stories.headline: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson fights to stay on 2027 ballot amid City Hall exodus, credit warning
stories.note: A Democrat-run flagship city's mayor is scrambling as staff flee and credit warnings pile up.
body: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson, a Democrat, is battling to keep his name on the ballot for the city's Feb. 23, 2027, mayoral election while his administration deals with a financial and staffing crisis.

Supporters of perennial candidate Willie Wilson have challenged more than 25,000 of Johnson's nominating signatures. He needs 12,500 valid ones. His campaign projects he will land around 14,788, but that is its own estimate, and the objectors say early rulings are going their way.

The ballot fight comes days after Johnson's third chief financial officer in 10 months, Ashlee Gabrysch, quit, saying staying would compromise her integrity. Standard & Poor's then put Chicago's BBB rating on negative watch, saying there is at least a 50% chance of a downgrade within 90 days, and the City Council voted 45-5 to review three years of city financial reporting for possible misstatements.

Johnson waved off the challenge, telling ABC 7 Chicago, "I'm going to be on the ballot." A September NORC survey put his approval at 22.2%, with 52.9% disapproving, and a 28-member council bloc says his tax plans for a $17.6 billion budget don't have the votes.

Why it matters: One of the country's most progressive big-city mayors is facing a credit warning, a revolving door in the finance office and dismal approval ratings, which makes him a ready-made example for Republicans of how Democratic city governments are run.

stories.headline: 2028 presidential contender under fire from state auditor over waste, fraud, abuse fears: 'Troubling response'
stories.note: Kentucky's auditor says possible 2028 Democratic candidate Andy Beshear brushed off $1.5 billion in waste her office found.
body: Kentucky Auditor Allison Ball says her office has found $1.5 billion in wasted taxpayer money across state government. She accuses Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, who is widely seen as a 2028 presidential hopeful, of brushing off the findings instead of helping fix them.

The largest item is $836 million in Medicaid spending, mostly from paying managed-care fees for people who were enrolled in Medicaid in up to eight other states at the same time. Her audits also found ineligible noncitizens getting benefits, single Social Security numbers used by as many as 10 people, duplicate payments, and about $100 million in SNAP errors.

Ball said that when she raised the Medicaid findings, the governor's office told her it happens everywhere. She called that "a troubling response." An earlier report also flagged spending by Beshear's executive branch, including a $7,632 limousine in Germany and a $17,013 distillery dinner.

Beshear's office has pushed back, calling the $836 million figure "a wild extrapolation from a small subset" and saying the actual overlap was smaller once the state could use updated federal databases.
Why it matters: Beshear is pitching himself as a competent red-state Democrat for 2028. A Republican auditor's list of waste and his office's dismissive answer give the GOP an early line of attack.

stories.headline: Dozens of FBI and DOJ personnel are investigating Peltola's Alaska victory
stories.note: Federal investigators are scrutinizing a Democratic win in Alaska.
body: Fox News reports that at least 50 FBI agents and more than a dozen Justice Department lawyers are investigating Alaska Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, a Democrat, over the alleged recruitment of a third candidate who shares the name of her opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The probe looks at whether Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee broke any laws in getting Daniel J. Sullivan, nicknamed "Decoy Dan," onto the ballot. The DOJ has reportedly sent more than 200 subpoenas and nearly 100 records-preservation letters, including one to Democratic elections lawyer Marc Elias, whose firm represents Peltola's campaign. A federal grand jury in Alaska meets monthly on the case.
An ally of Attorney General Todd Blanche told Fox News Digital that Blanche sees the alleged scheme as so egregious that he is putting major resources behind it. The DOJ itself declined to comment.

Peltola denies knowing anything about the recruitment, saying in October, "I am not interested in tricking voters." The DSCC also denies involvement. The AP projected her the winner with 144,486 votes to Sullivan's 131,965, with the other Sullivan and other minor candidates splitting 5,561 votes. Alaska targeted Nov. 25 for certification.
Why it matters: A full criminal investigation hangs over one of Democrats' biggest Senate pickups, and it keeps the "Decoy Dan" accusation in the headlines as Peltola heads to Washington.

stories.headline: Cruz turns tables on Democrats crying foul over GOP's 11th-hour judicial confirmation blitz
stories.note: Republicans keep locking in judges while they hold the Senate, and Cruz flips Democrats' complaints back on them.
body: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, accused Senate Democrats of hypocrisy for complaining that Republicans are rushing to confirm President Trump's judicial nominees before Democrats take over the Senate in January.

At a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Wednesday, where seven judicial nominees were introduced, Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., said that in 13 years he had never seen the committee hold back-to-back hearings without the minority's consent, and suggested waiting for the new Congress.

Cruz answered that after the 2024 election, Democrats confirmed 22 federal judges in November and December before Republicans took control, and that Booker and every other committee Democrat voted for all of them. He compared Booker to Captain Renault in "Casablanca," who is "shocked, shocked" to find gambling going on.

Booker said both parties have done this and that the Senate could have paused to do things "a right way." There are 27 federal judicial vacancies and 13 nominees waiting. Chuck Schumer, poised to become majority leader, has vowed to block Trump's nominees once Democrats hold the gavel.
Why it matters: Every judge Republicans confirm now serves for life, long after the current Senate majority is gone, and Cruz is making sure Democrats' own track record is on the record.

stories.headline: Texas Gov-elect Gina Hinojosa vows to rescind Abbott's H-1B visa restrictions despite admitting program abuse
stories.note: Texas' incoming Democratic governor wants to undo H-1B limits even while admitting the program is abused.
body: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, says she will rescind Gov. Greg Abbott's freeze on new H-1B visa petitions at state agencies and public universities on her first day in office, even though she admits the visa program is being abused.

Abbott's January order requires state agencies and public universities to get written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission before filing new H-1B petitions. He cited employers who fired American workers and replaced them with lower-paid foreign workers. The freeze was set to run through May 31, 2027, to give lawmakers time to pass reforms.

Speaking to the Texas Tribune, Hinojosa called the order a distraction, saying, "I'm not doing culture wars." In the same interview she said, "There are abuses when it comes to H-1Bs, absolutely," and objected to companies taking tax breaks and then hiring H-1B workers.

Hinojosa beat Abbott on Nov. 3 and is the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990. With Republicans still controlling the Texas Senate, undoing Abbott's executive orders is one of the few ways she can change policy without the legislature. Her office did not respond to Fox News Digital.

Why it matters: Texas' new Democratic governor is starting by rolling back a protection for American workers that she herself admits addresses a real problem, which gives Republicans a clear contrast to draw.

stories.headline: Mamdani’s plan to dismantle NYPD’s riot unit ripped as ‘smoke and mirrors’ by former force leaders
stories.note: Former NYPD leaders are blasting Mamdani's plan to scrap the riot unit.
body: Two former senior NYPD officials say New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to disband the department's Strategic Response Group, the unit that handles violent protests, is mostly a rebrand.

Mamdani wants to replace the SRG with a civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division that would stand between protesters and the uniformed officers who would still be on hand. Former NYPD Chief John Chell called it "nothing more than smoke and mirrors," and retired Inspector Paul Mauro said the main change is a new name with civilians inserted in front of the police.

Both men warned that waiting for civilians to call for help could delay police until a protest has already turned into a riot. Chell said officers who become reactive tend to hold back, which can get both officers and civilians hurt.

Mauro said the SRG's job was to calm and, if needed, control protests that were getting out of hand, and that it was deployed in only a small share of demonstrations. Mamdani's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Why it matters: Mamdani is keeping a progressive campaign promise on policing, and veteran police leaders say it either means nothing or puts people at risk. Either way, it gives Republicans more to say about public safety under the left.

stories.headline: Biden memoir draws fire for ‘denial’ as critics flag Gaza, racial-equity omissions
stories.note: Biden's memoir is getting panned for 'denial,' reopening old wounds for Democrats.
body: Former President Joe Biden's memoir, "Promise Me, America," released Nov. 17, is getting harsh reviews, including from outlets that usually lean left. Critics say it dodges the two biggest questions: his decision to run again in 2024 and his handling of the Gaza war.

The New Yorker's Amy Davidson Sorkin wrote that Biden is "as stubbornly in denial as ever." New York Times critic Jennifer Szalai said Biden gets "awkward and defensive" on those topics and portrays himself as a helpless victim of events.

According to the AP's review, Biden writes that he believed he was the best person to beat Donald Trump and that the primaries gave him no sign he was in trouble. Reviewers say he gives too little weight to concerns about his age, even while admitting his debate performance was poor.

Reviewers from Jacobin to the Times also faulted his account of his relationship with Israel. Semafor's David Weigel noted that the word "equity" never appears in the book, and that Biden leaves out his first-day order requiring DEI action plans across agencies.
Why it matters: Instead of moving past 2024, Democrats are once again arguing about Biden's age and his decision to stay in the race, and this time the criticism is coming from their own side.
